representation.reasoning: Helm counts 500 warriors and 179 women and children on the 12th (679; fact helm_count); the Missouri Gazette has about 800 at the giving out of the goods (fact gazette800). The town cannot draw hundreds, and a crowd of identical figures would misrepresent a camp of families. So: about one figure for every 16 people - 42 Potawatomi (12 named, 30 representative) - spread over the six camp grounds the 1812 records already draw, with the named chiefs at the grounds their cards give. Of the 42, 24 are men (57%), 10 women and 8 children: between Helm's 74% men and a family camp, because his count is of a war-time gathering and likely undercounts children (native.json). By day the men are partly away (hunting, fishing, at the factory and the council), so the camp itself shows mostly women, children and older people at work, which is what Currey's view from the fort (fact wigwams14) and Wau-Bun's 'camp ... where had been left their squaws and children' (fact camp_left) describe. The Miami escort is about 30 (Heald), 27 (Helm) or fifteen (Wau-Bun): 8 are drawn (about one in four), so the party still reads as a mounted escort.
representation.miami: a bivouac on open ground south-west of the fort (about E 1100, N 165), horses picketed just south of it (E 1097, N 150): reconstructed; no source places the Miami camp.

conflicts_and_choices: Wells's arrival: Heald 13th (followed), Helm 12th, Wau-Bun and Currey 14th. The battle jaunt's 'the-gate' stop (14 Aug, sunset) follows Wau-Bun. Each Miami card carries alt_days for the 14th arrival; the owner decides.
The goods: Wau-Bun 13th, Heald 14th. Both jaunt stops are honoured: cloth on the afternoon of the 13th, the rest and the provisions on the morning of the 14th.
The council of the 14th is Wau-Bun's alone (family tradition); its place is not given and is put on the esplanade where the 12th's council sat.

Black Partridge's visit: Helm (contemporary) 'the night of the 14th'; Wau-Bun 'the evening succeeding the council'. Placed 19:45-20:45. Wau-Bun's speech for him is not attested dialogue (Quaife App. II) and is not staged; the battle jaunt's 'the-gate' stop quotes it, which the owner may want reviewed.
The Miami camp place, every lodge assignment, every hour and every task are reconstructed.
implementer_notes: People of this group are 'indoors' only inside a camp lodge (where = a potawatomi_camp_1812_* id) or in the commanding officer's quarters; a visitor knocking at a ground's lodges can ask for anyone whose span is indoors there.
Meals are outdoors under the arbors (an August camp cooks out of doors): this departs from the brief's 'meals indoors' on purpose.
Spans with activity 'paddle' cross the main river by canoe; if the town cannot draw a canoe, hide the card for those spans. Spans 'away (not drawn)' hide the card.
The Miami sleep in the open (activity 'sleep'): if there is no lying pose, hide them while asleep.

Routes are via points on the 1812 ground, checked against every 1812 footprint (both senses of each record's rotation) and the e1830_natural heightfield; the walks cross the creek's shallow swale (about 0.5 m deep) at E 762-806.

Each standing point is at least 0.6 m clear of camp gear and buildings and 0.85 m from anyone else standing at the same time in this file; the other four researchers' people (Heald, Wells, Kinzie, the soldiers at the gate and the wharf) still need a cross-check.

bases.night_in_lodge: Night in the lodge. The lodges are the camp records of August 1812 (L-1812-potawatomi-camp-2515), which give no lodge to a family; which lodge this card sleeps in is this reading's. Sleeping indoors at night is ordinary camp life, not recorded for this night.
bases.camp_work: Ordinary work of a family camp in late summer at the yard the camp records draw (hearth, arbor, racks, mortar, hide frame, woodpile). That the camp held families is attested (facts helm_count, camp_left); this person's task and hour are this reading's.
bases.meal_at_arbor: Cooking and eating at the yard's hearth under its bough arbor, the arrangement the camp records take from Forsyth and Skinner. In August a camp cooks and eats out of doors, so meals here are outdoors, not indoors. The hours are this reading's; no source gives them.
bases.walk_camp_fort: Walking between the camp and the fort on the south bank; the path is this reading's, checked clear of the 1812 buildings and the river. It steps across the creek's shallow swale where the camp is on its far side.
bases.goods_14_aug: Heald, writing in October 1812, gives the factory goods and spare provisions out on the 14th (fact goods14). The hour, and who went to the factory, are this reading's; nothing of the giving out is staged beyond people waiting and carrying.
bases.council_14_aug: Wau-Bun has a second council on the afternoon of the 14th (fact council14). Its place is not given; it is put on the esplanade where the council of the 12th sat (fact esplanade). Who sat in it, and the hours, are this reading's. No speech, pipe or ceremony is staged.
bases.evening_at_yard: Evening at the yard after the day's meal, before the lodges are closed for the night. Reconstructed from camp routine; no source describes this evening in the camp.
bases.council_12_aug: Wau-Bun puts a council with the assembled people on the afternoon of the 12th, on the esplanade under the blockhouses (facts council12, esplanade). Who of this card's people sat in it is this reading's; no speech is staged.
bases.goods_13_aug: Wau-Bun gives out the factory goods on the 13th (fact goods13); Heald gives them on the 14th (fact goods14). This reading shows cloth going out on the afternoon of the 13th and the rest of the goods and the provisions on the morning of the 14th, so both jaunt stops (battle-of-fort-dearborn "factory", 13 Aug 14:00; first-fort-dearborn-tour "agency", 14 Aug 16:30, shelves bare) find what they say.
bases.day_15_men_away: 15 August: the men went south with the column (Heald; Wau-Bun). This reading stages nothing of the battle: the card is not drawn in the town from 7:30 to 13:00, and the battle jaunt carries that morning.
bases.basis_1: 15 August: the women and children had stayed at the camp near the fort (fact camp_left). Ordinary work is drawn; the prisoners brought to the camp that afternoon (Wau-Bun) are not staged by this reading, and the owner decides whether the camp is drawn at all on the 15th.
bases.canoe_crossing: Crossing the main river by canoe between the creek mouth and the Kinzie landing. Canoes are drawn up on the camp's mouth ground (the camp records); the crossing and its hours are this reading's. If the town cannot draw a canoe, hide the card while it is on the water.
bases.day_16_aug: 16 August, the morning the fort was burned (Wau-Bun): the camp still stands (to the 16th, L-1812-potawatomi-camp-2515); ordinary work only is drawn.
bases.basis_2: Kinzie's friends among the chiefs (Topenebe, Kee-po-tah, Waubansee: Wau-Bun ch. XIX; native.json) seeing him at the fort, where his family had lived since April. The visit is this reading's; nothing they said is known or staged.
bases.day_15_camp: 15 August: the women and children stayed at the camp near the fort (fact camp_left). Ordinary work is drawn; the prisoners brought to the camp that afternoon (Wau-Bun) are not staged by this reading, and the owner decides whether the camp is drawn at all on the 15th.
bases.basis_3: A camp of some 700 people needed meat; men hunting at dawn is ordinary camp life. Not recorded for this day.
bases.away_winter: Away at the winter hunting grounds and the spring sugar camps: Juliette Kinzie saw villages left for the wintering-grounds and re-occupied in spring (fact wintering, 1831). Not drawn.
bases.ordinary_visit: Before 1812 the Potawatomi came and went at Chicago by habit (Currey, fact come_go), camping on the State Street creek (fact camping) and bringing furs and maple sugar to the traders (fact sugar). A family of three coming by canoe on a trading day is this reading's; the camp records stand only 12-16 August 1812, so on other dates no lodge is drawn and the visitors are drawn by day only. Visits are on about one day in five in the trading seasons (the implementer may seed which days from the date).

potawatomi_man_1812.pieces: Breechcloth of dark blue (or red) stroud, its ends hanging front and back over a belt; leggings of blue or red stroud (some of smoked deerskin), reaching from ankle to upper thigh and tied to the belt, the seam or a broad flap on the outside, gartered below the knee; a loose trade shirt of checked or striped linen or printed calico, short, worn outside the breechcloth (Keating: "a short checkered shirt over it"); a wool blanket worn as a mantle, or belted at the waist and hung from the shoulders (Keating), set aside in the heat of the day; moccasins of smoked deerskin, centre-seam or puckered toe, some with turned-down ankle cuffs; a finger-woven or cloth sash or a leather belt carrying a knife in a sheath, a pouch, flint and steel; a tobacco pouch. Hair long and tied or clubbed behind, a few men with a lock and feathers on a string (Keating, Metea 1823) or a handkerchief tied round the head (a minority: the cloth turbans of the 1830s pictures are later and are not general in 1812). Ornament: silver ear-bobs, one or two silver armbands or wristbands, a few brooches on the shirt (Wau-Bun's list of the trade silver). Paint: a few men with a touch of vermilion round an eye or on the cheek (Keating 1823) - fresh paint was among the goods given out (Wau-Bun). No war paint on the 12th-14th: the black paint of the 15th (Wau-Bun) is not drawn before it. A gun only on the hunters going out and coming in, and at the lodges.
potawatomi_man_1812.colours: dark indigo and scarlet stroud with the undyed white selvage showing; white, blue and red blankets; checked blue-and-white, red-and-white or brown linen shirts; printed calico; smoked-tan moccasins; bright silver
potawatomi_man_1812.not: NOT generic Plains dress: no feathered war bonnet, no fringed and beaded buckskin war shirt or full hide suit, no tipi, no travois, no horned headdress. These are Great Lakes people of 1812 dressed largely in trade cloth.
potawatomi_man_1812.grade_note: inferred for the pieces (Keating 1823 at Fort Wayne, eleven years later and a hundred and fifty miles off; Hubbard 1818; the trade lists); reconstructed for colours, proportions and how many men wear which.

potawatomi_chief_1812.pieces: As potawatomi_man_1812, with more silver: several armbands and wristbands, a silver gorget or a peace medal on a ribbon or thong (Black Partridge's Greenville medal until he gives it up at 20:45 on the 14th; its type is unattested - a plain oval silver medal or none), more brooches set on the shirt, a better blanket or a blue broadcloth match-coat. Black Partridge: a gold ring in the nose (Andreas, unsourced there). Some chiefs may wear a trade coat; Lewis's 1826-27 portraits show coats, but they are later and treaty dress.
potawatomi_chief_1812.colours: as potawatomi_man_1812, with blue broadcloth and more silver
potawatomi_chief_1812.not: NOT generic Plains dress: no feathered war bonnet, no fringed and beaded buckskin war shirt or full hide suit, no tipi, no travois, no horned headdress. These are Great Lakes people of 1812 dressed largely in trade cloth.
potawatomi_chief_1812.grade_note: The medal and nose ring are the only ornaments recorded for a named man (Helm; Andreas). The rest is the man's dress with more silver, which Wau-Bun's trade lists and the later portraits support.

potawatomi_elder_1812.pieces: As potawatomi_man_1812, the blanket worn more often, a plainer shirt; grey hair; a staff for Topenebe.
potawatomi_elder_1812.not: NOT generic Plains dress: no feathered war bonnet, no fringed and beaded buckskin war shirt or full hide suit, no tipi, no travois, no horned headdress. These are Great Lakes people of 1812 dressed largely in trade cloth.

potawatomi_woman_1812.pieces: A wrapped skirt of dark blue (or black) stroud, a length of cloth wrapped round the waist and held by a belt or tie, reaching to mid-calf, the white selvage at the hem, some edged with a narrow band of silk ribbon (the full ribbonwork of the 1830s-40s pictures is later and is not drawn); a loose over-blouse of printed calico or checked cloth to the hips, sleeves to the wrist or elbow, with a few silver brooches; leggings of red or blue stroud to the knee; moccasins of smoked deerskin; a blanket or shawl over the shoulders or drawn over the head (Currey: heads covered with blankets). Hair parted in the middle and worn long, tied or clubbed at the back. Ornaments: strings of glass beads, silver ear-bobs, brooches. A mother carries her infant in a cradleboard (Wau-Bun's "toy-models of Indian cradles" were sold by the women), on her back or set upright beside her work. Burdens are carried on the back. On the 13th-14th some cloth is new from the factory (blankets, broadcloths, calicoes: Wau-Bun; Heald).
potawatomi_woman_1812.colours: dark blue skirts; red or blue leggings; calico in reds, pinks, blues and small prints; white or blue blankets; beads white, blue and red; silver
potawatomi_woman_1812.not: NOT generic Plains dress: no feathered war bonnet, no fringed and beaded buckskin war shirt or full hide suit, no tipi, no travois, no horned headdress. These are Great Lakes people of 1812 dressed largely in trade cloth. No fringed and beaded buckskin dress.
potawatomi_woman_1812.grade_note: No 1812 description of a Potawatomi woman's dress at Chicago was found (native.json). Built from the trade goods (Wau-Bun ch. II; the goods of the 13th), Quaife's 1833 synthesis ("The squaws wore blue or printed cotton cloths"), Winter's 1837 picture of Sin-is-quaw (Potawatomi, Indiana), and a Miami woman's pair of wool and ribbon leggings of about 1820 (DIA). Wau-Bun's gala dress of the Ho-Chunk at Fort Winnebago (1830: blue broadcloth petticoat, scarlet leggings, rows of brooches) is a festival dress of a neighbouring people and is not used for workday dress.

potawatomi_elder_woman_1812.pieces: As potawatomi_woman_1812, plainer and more faded; the blanket worn more; grey hair.
potawatomi_elder_woman_1812.not: NOT generic Plains dress: no feathered war bonnet, no fringed and beaded buckskin war shirt or full hide suit, no tipi, no travois, no horned headdress. These are Great Lakes people of 1812 dressed largely in trade cloth.

potawatomi_child_1812.pieces: Small children in a calico or linen shirt to the knee; girls from about seven dressed as their mothers in small (skirt, blouse, leggings), a kerchief on the head of some; boys a breechcloth and shirt, leggings on the older boys; many barefoot in August, others in moccasins. An infant in a cradleboard wrapped in cloth.
potawatomi_child_1812.colours: calico prints, checked linen, blue and red stroud
potawatomi_child_1812.not: NOT generic Plains dress: no feathered war bonnet, no fringed and beaded buckskin war shirt or full hide suit, no tipi, no travois, no horned headdress. These are Great Lakes people of 1812 dressed largely in trade cloth.
potawatomi_child_1812.grade_note: From Winter's 1837 picture of a girl in a calico shirt, leggings and head kerchief and an infant in a blue gown; nothing earlier was found.

miami_escort_1812.pieces: Mounted men on a hard ride and an escort duty: a trade shirt of calico or checked linen; breechcloth and stroud leggings with side flaps; moccasins; a blanket rolled behind the saddle, or a hooded capote (Keating: a Miami leader at Fort Wayne in 1823 wore a capote in place of the blanket); a cloth or fur head-wrap on some, a handkerchief on others; silver armbands and wristbands, silver ear ornaments, a nose ring on some (Lewis's Mi-a-qu-a, a Miami chief taken at the Mississinewa treaty, shows broad silver armbands over the sleeves, a nose ring, ear pendants, a silver gorget and a dark turban with a feather - treaty dress fourteen years on, so the gorget and coat are kept to one or two men). A gun (musket or rifle), powder horn and shot pouch on each man: an armed escort. Ponies with pad or wooden saddles and rope or hide bridles. On the march of the 15th Wells himself blackened his face (Wau-Bun); the escort's paint on the 15th is not recorded and is not drawn.
miami_escort_1812.colours: as potawatomi_man_1812; dark blue coats and red cloth on one or two; much silver
miami_escort_1812.not: NOT generic Plains dress: no feathered war bonnet, no fringed and beaded buckskin war shirt or full hide suit, no tipi, no travois, no horned headdress. These are Great Lakes people of 1812 dressed largely in trade cloth.
miami_escort_1812.grade_note: No source describes the escort's dress. The Miami and Potawatomi of the Wabash and St Joseph wore the same Great Lakes trade-cloth dress in these years; Lewis (1826-27) and Keating (1823) give the Miami particulars.
